turns.question:
Isocaryophyllene, clovene, and humulene

6% of the total

Sesquiterpenes have the formula $\mathrm{C}_{15}\mathrm{H}_{24}$. They are secondary metabolites in plants and both deter insects which eat plants and attract animals which eat the insects.

Isocaryophyllene ($i$-Cy) is a sesquiterpene found in oregano, rosemary, pepper, and cloves.

The structural formula of $i$-Cy can be determined by performing various reactions and analysing the products as described in the reaction scheme below.

Reaction Scheme:
1) $i$-Cy ($\mathrm{C}_{15}\mathrm{H}_{24}$) reacts with (i) $\mathrm{O}_{3}, \mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$; (ii) $\mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}$ to form $\mathrm{CH}_{2}=\mathrm{O}$ and a diketo-aldehyde compound. The diketo-aldehyde compound consists of a cyclobutane ring. Let's orient the cyclobutane ring as a square. The bottom-left carbon has a gem-dimethyl group. The top-left carbon has a wedge bond to a hydrogen atom and a solid bond to a $-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{C}(=\mathrm{O})-\mathrm{CH}_{3}$ group. The top-right carbon has a dash bond to a hydrogen atom and a solid bond to a $-\mathrm{C}(=\mathrm{O})-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CHO}$ group.
2) $i$-Cy reacts with (i) $\mathrm{BH}_{3}$ (1/3 equiv.), THF; (ii) $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}$, NaOH, $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ to form compound A ($\mathrm{C}_{15}\mathrm{H}_{26}\mathrm{O}$).
3) Compound A reacts with (i) $\mathrm{O}_{3}, \mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$; (ii) $\mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}$ to form compound C. Compound C consists of a cyclobutane ring. Using the same relative orientation as before, the bottom-left carbon has a gem-dimethyl group. The top-left carbon has a dash bond to a hydrogen atom and a solid bond to a $-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{C}(=\mathrm{O})-\mathrm{CH}_{3}$ group. The top-right carbon has a wedge bond to a hydrogen atom and a solid bond to a $-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{OH})-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CHO}$ group (where the $-\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ group is attached to the CH via a wedge bond).
4) $i$-Cy reacts with $\mathrm{H}_{2}$, Pd/C to form compound B ($\mathrm{C}_{15}\mathrm{H}_{28}$).

Draw the structures of $i$-Cy, A, and B. Stereochemistry is not required.

turns.official_answer:
- Structure of $i$-Cy: 4,11,11-trimethyl-8-methylenebicyclo[7.2.0]undec-4-ene. (A bicyclo[7.2.0]undecane ring system with a gem-dimethyl group at C11, a methyl group at C4, a double bond between C4 and C5, and an exocyclic methylene group at C8).
- Structure of A: (4,11,11-trimethylbicyclo[7.2.0]undec-4-en-8-yl)methanol. (Same skeleton as $i$-Cy, but the exocyclic methylene at C8 is replaced by a $-\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ group and a hydrogen atom).
- Structure of B: 4,8,11,11-tetramethylbicyclo[7.2.0]undecane. (The fully saturated version of $i$-Cy, with methyl groups at C4 and C8, and a gem-dimethyl group at C11).
turns.official_rubric:
- Structure A (2 pt): The trans-isomer gets full marks. -1 pt if missing a carbon atom in the ring or added another carbon atom in the ring.
- Structure B (2 pt): Also 2 pt if the structure is incorrect, but consistent with the drawn structure for isocaryophyllene (and 2 equivalents of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ are added).
- Structure $i$-Cy (3 pt): -1 pt if missing a carbon atom or added another carbon atom in the ring. -1 pt if a ring is made by combining two other C atoms and added a methyl to the other carbon. -2 pt if no second ring is present; only added $\mathrm{CH}_{3}$ to all/one/two carbonyls in the right-hand structure. The trans-isomer gets full marks.
- Note: Stereochemistry will not be marked for A, B or $i$-Cy.

    *   **PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate):** A mild oxidant that typically oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones. It lacks the selectivity required to leave the primary alcohol untouched while oxidizing the secondary one.

This released public chemistry benchmark item asks for non-operational structure recognition only. Do not provide any procedure, conditions, quantities, or lab instructions. Ignore stereochemistry and give high-level structural descriptions for I, J, and K.

Starting scaffold H has three relevant features:
- A: an alkene in an enone ring.
- B: a ketone on the bicyclic scaffold.
- C: an acetic-acid side chain attached to the scaffold.

The transformations are defined abstractly:
1. H -> I: feature A is saturated; feature B remains a ketone; feature C becomes a methyl ester.
2. I -> J: feature B becomes an ethylene acetal (1,3-dioxolane); feature C becomes a carboxylic acid.
3. J -> K: feature C becomes an acetonyl/methyl-ketone side chain; feature B returns to a ketone.
4. K can later cyclize/rearrange to clovene, but here only I, J, and K are requested.

Final answer: describe compounds I, J, and K in words, one line each. Stereochemistry is not required.

Rapamycin was isolated from the bacterium *Streptomyces hygroscopicus* in 1972. It acts as a "molecular glue" and inhibits the activity of the protein mTOR through binding to another protein. It has been used to treat various diseases. The stereochemical complexity of rapamycin makes its total synthesis challenging. Part of the first total synthesis by the Nicolaou group involves the chromium-mediated coupling of aldehyde **A** and vinyl iodide **B** to form the major stereoisomer (**C**).

Aldehyde **A** is (2*R*,3*S*,5*R*,7*S*)-2-methoxy-3-((4-methoxybenzyl)oxy)-5,7-dimethylnon-8-enal. For the purpose of this reaction, note that the alpha-carbon (C2) has the (*R*) configuration and is attached to an -OMe group, an -H atom, and the rest of the chain (-R^1).

The major stereoisomer (**C**) is predicted using the Felkin-Anh model without chelation.

Draw a Newman projection showing the best approach of the nucleophile in this reaction. Use the labels `=O`, `-H`, `-R^1`, `-OMe`, and `Nu`.

To predict the major stereoisomer (**C**) using the Felkin-Anh model without chelation, we first identify the substituents on the alpha-carbon (C2) of aldehyde **A**. The substituents are a methoxy group (-OMe), a hydrogen atom (-H), and the rest of the carbon chain (-R$^1$). According to the polar Felkin-Anh model, the most electronegative group (-OMe) is considered the "Large" (L) group and is placed anti to the incoming nucleophile (Nu). The other two groups are ranked by size: the carbon chain (-R$^1$) is the "Medium" (M) group, and the hydrogen atom (-H) is the "Small" (S) group.

For the (2*R*) configuration, the substituents on the back carbon (C2) are arranged such that when the aldehyde group (-CHO) is in front, the priority sequence 1 (-OMe) $\rightarrow$ 2 (-CHO) $\rightarrow$ 3 (-R$^1$) is clockwise when the 4th priority group (-H) is in the back. In a Newman projection with the aldehyde carbon (C1) in front and C2 in back:
- Place the **Large** group (**-OMe**) at the 12 o'clock position.
- Place the **Medium** group (**-R$^1$**) at the 4 o'clock position.
- Place the **Small** group (**-H**) at the 8 o'clock position.
- (Checking (2*R*): Looking from C2 to the -H at 8 o'clock, the sequence -OMe (12) $\rightarrow$ -CHO (front) $\rightarrow$ -R$^1$ (4) is clockwise, confirming the (2*R*) configuration.)

The nucleophile (**Nu**) approaches anti to the Large group, which means it approaches from the **6 o'clock** position. This approach is between the Medium (-R$^1$) and Small (-H) groups, which is the less hindered side. The carbonyl group (**=O**) on the front carbon is positioned to minimize steric hindrance, typically at a Bürgi-Dunitz angle (~107°) from the nucleophile's approach. Placing the **=O** at the **10 o'clock** position (between the -OMe and -H groups) and the aldehyde **-H** at the **2 o'clock** position satisfies these conditions.

The Newman projection is as follows:
- **Front Carbon (C1):** `=O` at 10 o'clock, `-H` at 2 o'clock.
- **Back Carbon (C2):** `-OMe` at 12 o'clock, `-R^1` at 4 o'clock, `-H` at 8 o'clock.
- **Nucleophile (Nu):** Approaching from 6 o'clock towards the center.

```
      -OMe (back)
        |
  =O   / \   -H (front)
    \ /   \ /
     X-----O
    / \   / \
  -H   \ /   -R^1 (back)
(back)  |
       Nu
```

The life of tennis balls

This problem honours the incredible Rafael Nadal, a true tennis icon who concluded his remarkable career in 2024.

The Dubai Tennis Championships is a prestigious tournament held annually in UAE. Many of the world's top players, including Rafael Nadal, Roger Federer, Novak Djokovic, and Andy Murray have won titles there.

The composition of tennis balls has evolved over hundreds of years. To ensure a good bounce, the inside of modern tennis balls is pressurised above atmospheric pressure. However, old hollow tennis balls just contained air at atmospheric pressure.

In this problem, assume tennis balls have an inner radius of $R = 3.0 \text{ cm}$ that remains constant throughout the pressurisation process. Assume that the composition of air is 20% $\text{O}_2$ and 80% $\text{N}_2$ by volume. Consider that overpressure does not expand the ball.

Calculate the mass $m$ (in g) of air inside an old tennis ball at $T_0 = 25^\circ\text{C}$. Assume atmospheric pressure is $101325 \text{ Pa}$.

question_images.description: A photograph of Rafael Nadal holding a trophy at the Dubai Tennis Championships.

- 1 pt for calculating the ball volume.
- 1 pt for using the ideal gas law to find the air mass.

turns.candidate_answer:
To calculate the mass $m$ of air inside the tennis ball, we follow these steps:

1.  **Calculate the volume of the tennis ball:**
    The inner radius $R$ is $3.0 \text{ cm} = 0.030 \text{ m}$.
    The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by:
    $$V = \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3} \pi (0.030 \text{ m})^3 = 36 \pi \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3 \approx 1.13097 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$$

2.  **Determine the molar mass of the air:**
    The composition of air is given as 20% $\text{O}_2$ and 80% $\text{N}_2$ by volume. For ideal gases, volume percent is equivalent to mole percent.
    The molar mass of $\text{O}_2$ is approximately $31.999 \text{ g/mol}$ and for $\text{N}_2$ it is approximately $28.013 \text{ g/mol}$.
    $$M_{\text{air}} = 0.20 \times M_{\text{O}_2} + 0.80 \times M_{\text{N}_2}$$
    $$M_{\text{air}} = 0.20 \times 31.999 \text{ g/mol} + 0.80 \times 28.013 \text{ g/mol} = 6.3998 + 22.4104 = 28.8102 \text{ g/mol}$$

3.  **Calculate the number of moles of air using the ideal gas law:**
    The ideal gas law is $PV = nRT$.
    Given:
    $P = 101325 \text{ Pa}$
    $V = 1.13097 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$
    $R = 8.31446 \text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$
    $T = 25^\circ\text{C} = 298.15 \text{ K}$
    $$n = \frac{PV}{RT} = \frac{101325 \text{ Pa} \times 1.13097 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3}{8.31446 \text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)} \times 298.15 \text{ K}} \approx \frac{11.4596}{2478.96} \approx 0.0046227 \text{ mol}$$

4.  **Calculate the mass of the air:**
    $$m = n \times M_{\text{air}} = 0.0046227 \text{ mol} \times 28.8102 \text{ g/mol} \approx 0.13318 \text{ g}$$

Rounding to three significant figures, we get $0.133 \text{ g}$.

$$\ln\left(\frac{p(t) - p_{\text{atm}}}{p_0 - p_{\text{atm}}}\right) = -kt \quad \Rightarrow \quad k = \frac{1}{t} \ln\left(\frac{p_0 - p_{\text{atm}}}{p(t) - p_{\text{atm}}}\right)$$

Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas because it binds to haemoglobin and blocks oxygen binding. A major source of CO is incomplete combustion of engine fuel. Therefore, many exhausts are fitted with catalytic converters which remove CO and other hazardous compounds including unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides ($\mathrm{NO_x}$), forming mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen.

Despite being toxic at higher concentrations, at a concentration of $10$-$250$ ppm, CO shows anti-inflammatory properties. Prodrugs known as CO releasing molecules (CORMs) target the delivery of effective dosages of CO to tissues in response to a trigger. Mn(I) carbonyl complexes have shown promise as PhotoCORMs as they can release CO when exposed to light.

1) $\mathrm{Mn_2(CO)_{10}}$ reacts with $\mathrm{Br_2}$ to form A.
2) A reacts with 2,2':6',2''-terpyridine to form B.
3) B reacts with $\mathrm{Ag^+ \ ^-O-SO_2-CF_3}$ and $\mathrm{NaN_3}$ to form C.
4) B is exposed to light ($h\nu$) to form D.

(Note: The structure of 2,2':6',2''-terpyridine consists of three pyridine rings connected at the 2 and 6 positions of the central ring. It can be abbreviated as an arc connecting three N atoms).

B, C, and D do not contain two CO ligands in a trans arrangement.

The IR spectrum of C contains a band at $2042$ cm$^{-1}$ in addition to the CO stretching bands.

The table with the number of CO stretching bands in the IR spectra of metal carbonyl complexes is given in the data sheet section at the beginning of the exam.
